evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14: quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī
terms.comment: Inborn ability, as against what is learned: ingenium beside studium (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14) or doctrīna. Talented is ingeniōsus (Traupman 32, 158, 390); in the plural ingenia are talented people: scrīptōrum magna ingenia (Sall. Cat. 8.3).

evidence: Cic. Sen. 26: adulēscentēs bonā indole praeditī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Inborn character and talents, especially the promise of the young (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Quod tibi plānē deest, mī fīlī, nōn est ingenium sed ambitiō!
phrases.english: What you plainly lack, my son, is not ability but ambition!

phrases.latin: dē ejus ērudītiōne quod labōrēs nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī, studium ego videō.
phrases.english: About his education you have nothing to worry about: his ability you know, and his application I can see.
so talents are often lost through bad luck
